blocks.md: Each sample of data gives a slightly different regression estimate, just as each poll gives a slightly different answer. The sampling distribution describes how those estimates would be spread out if you could repeat the sampling many times: centred on the true value, with a spread that shrinks as the sample grows. Because the true spread is unknown, it is estimated from the residuals, and that extra uncertainty is why test statistics follow a t distribution instead of a normal.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It is what turns a single estimate into a statement of confidence — standard errors, t tests and confidence intervals all come from it.

Why this is immediate: $b_2 = \beta_2 + \sum w_i e_i$ is a linear combination of normals, and a linear transformation of a normal vector is normal. In matrix form, $\mathbf{b} = \boldsymbol{\beta} + (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$, so if $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I})$ then $\mathbf{b}\sim N(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1})$.
The CLT makes the above **approximately** correct for large $N$. See [Error Normality and Jarque-Bera](note:error-normality-and-jarque-bera).

**Why $N-2$, not $N$.** The two normal equations impose two exact linear restrictions on the $N$ residuals ($\sum\hat{e}_i = 0$ and $\sum x_i\hat{e}_i = 0$), so only $N-2$ are free. In matrix terms $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ and
so dividing by $N-K$ makes $\widehat{\sigma}^2$ unbiased. See [Projection Matrix and Residual Maker](note:projection-matrix-and-residual-maker). Dividing by $N$ would understate $\sigma^2$.
Substitute $\widehat{\sigma}^2$ into the variance formulas from [OLS Estimator](note:ols-estimator):

**Why $t$ and not normal**: you replaced the unknown $\sigma$ with an estimate built from the same data. If $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and $V\sim\chi^2_
u$ independently, then $Z/\sqrt{V/
u}\sim t_
u$. Here $(N-2)\widehat{\sigma}^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{N-2}$, and it is **independent** of $b_2$ — a consequence of $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{0}$.
The default software null is $H_0: \beta_k = 0$ two-sided. A small $p$-value rejects, meaning the coefficient is statistically distinguishable from zero — **not** that it is economically meaningful.

One- and two-sided tests, p-values and worked examples: [Hypothesis Tests on Regression Coefficients](note:hypothesis-tests-on-regression-coefficients). The fit statistic $R^2$: [Coefficient of Determination](note:coefficient-of-determination).
